paragraphs.heading: What it measures
paragraphs.text: Solar irradiance is how much power from the Sun lands on each patch of area, carried as electromagnetic radiation within whatever wavelengths the instrument can detect. It is given in watts per square metre, written W/m². If you add it up over a stretch of time, you get the energy that arrived on each square metre during that time, in joules per square metre. That running total goes by several names, including solar irradiation, solar exposure and insolation.

paragraphs.heading: Where you measure matters
paragraphs.text: Irradiance can be measured out in space or down at the ground, after the air has absorbed and scattered some of the light. In space, the reading depends on how far you are from the Sun, on the solar cycle, and on changes that run across cycles. At the ground, three more things count: how the measuring surface is tilted, how high the Sun stands above the horizon, and the state of the air. The numbers matter well beyond the lab, since sunlight shapes how plants run their chemistry and how animals behave, and measurements help forecast solar power output, plan heating and cooling for buildings, model climate, predict weather and plan space travel.

paragraphs.heading: Direct and scattered light
paragraphs.text: Scientists split sunlight into parts. Total solar irradiance, or TSI, counts every wavelength arriving at the top of Earth's atmosphere, on a surface turned square to the incoming sunlight. Direct normal irradiance, or DNI, is the beam coming straight from the Sun, measured face-on, leaving out light that the air has scattered or reflected. It equals the light above the atmosphere minus what the air absorbs and scatters on the way down, and those losses change with the time of day, cloud cover, moisture and other contents of the air. Diffuse horizontal irradiance, or DHI, is the scattered share: light coming from across the sky and caught on a flat surface. With no atmosphere, there would be almost none of it.

paragraphs.heading: Panels and units
paragraphs.text: For solar power plants, a key figure is global tilted irradiance, the total light falling on a surface set at a chosen tilt and direction, whether fixed or turning to follow the Sun. It often serves as a reference for photovoltaic power plants. The solar power industry usually counts insolation in kilowatt hours per square metre (kWh/m²). Another unit for insolation, the langley, is defined as one thermochemical calorie on each square centimetre, which comes to 41,840 J/m².

paragraphs.heading: From 1361 to 340
paragraphs.text: At the top of Earth's atmosphere, sunlight arrives at about 1361 W/m², averaged over the year. Seen from the Sun, Earth looks like a roughly circular disc of area πr², where r is Earth's radius, and that disc catches a fairly steady 1361 W/m² at all times. But Earth is close to a sphere, with a total surface of 4πr². Spread over the whole globe, through the day and across the year, the incoming sunlight therefore averages a quarter of that figure, about 340 W/m².

paragraphs.heading: Seasons and ice ages
paragraphs.text: How sunlight is spread over the top of the atmosphere is set by Earth's round shape and the details of its orbit. Knowing that pattern is essential for numerical weather prediction and for understanding the seasons and changes in climate. Applied to the ice ages, the same idea is known as the Milankovitch cycles.
